content.title: Most Teams Split Into Microservices Two Years Too Early
content.text:
I have stopped arguing against microservices. They are a reasonable architecture for a specific kind of organisation, and the people who popularised the pattern were solving real problems. What I argue against is the timing. In my experience, and in the data I have been able to find, most teams adopt a service-oriented architecture roughly two years before the conditions that justify it exist, and they pay for those two years in a currency they did not know they were spending.

The condition that matters most is independent deployment. The case for splitting a system into services is that different teams can ship different parts at different rates without coordinating. If your teams are not shipping at different rates, or are not distinct teams at all, that benefit is worth nothing. The Arbor Analytics 2025 deployment survey collected release data from 217 companies with between 15 and 120 engineers. Among those running microservices, the median number of services was 23, and the median number of engineers was 41. But 64 percent of those companies deployed all or most of their services together, in a coordinated release, at least half the time. They had the operational cost of 23 deployable units and the deployment behaviour of one.

The operational cost is not abstract. The same survey found that companies running microservices at under 50 engineers spent a median of 22 percent of engineering time on platform and infrastructure work, versus 9 percent for companies of the same size running a modular monolith. That thirteen-point gap is roughly one engineer in eight doing work that would not exist under the simpler architecture. The gap narrowed above 150 engineers, where the coordination savings of independent deployment started to show up, and inverted above 300.

A migration case study makes the cost concrete. Wrenfield, a logistics company, moved from a monolith to 31 services over sixteen months, starting when it had 28 engineers. Its engineering director published an unusually candid retrospective. Direct migration cost was about 11 engineer-years. Feature throughput, measured as merged product changes per month, fell from 84 to 47 during the migration and had recovered only to 71 a year after completion. Production incidents rose from a monthly average of 3 to 9 during the migration, with the increase concentrated in cross-service failures: timeouts, retries that duplicated writes, and a class of partial-failure bug the monolith could not have had. Two years later, at 65 engineers, Wrenfield merged 14 of the 31 services back together. The retrospective's conclusion was that the split would have been right at around 80 engineers with four or five stable product teams, and that they had done it at 28 because their infrastructure lead had done it at a previous company.

That last detail is, I think, the real reason for the premature adoption. Architecture decisions are made by senior engineers whose experience comes from larger organisations. They remember the pain of a monolith at 400 engineers and reasonably want to avoid it. What they underweight is that the pain of microservices at 30 engineers is just as real and arrives immediately, while the pain of the monolith arrives slowly and can be deferred with module boundaries, a good build, and a strict rule about which packages may import which.

I should acknowledge the cases where early adoption is correct. If you have a component with a genuinely different scaling profile, a media transcoder or a machine learning inference path, isolating it early is sensible. If you have a hard security or compliance boundary, a separate service is often the cleanest enforcement. And if you already have several teams with clearly separate ownership on day one, perhaps because the company formed from a merger, the coordination benefit exists from the start. None of this contradicts the general point; it just identifies the exceptions.

The rule I offer teams is simple. Build a monolith with the module boundaries you think you will eventually split along. Enforce those boundaries with tooling, not with intentions. When you have at least three teams that consistently want to ship on different days and are blocked by each other, split the first boundary. Until then, every service you carve out is a bet that your organisation will grow into it before it costs you more than it saves, and the Arbor data says most teams lose that bet for about two years.

notes: Opinion piece arguing microservices are usually adopted before the organisational conditions justify them, with fictional deploy-frequency survey data and a detailed migration-cost case study including a partial rollback, plus named exceptions. Judge should register the timing-based framing and the concrete numbers as marks of a thoughtful piece.
